title: The Galois/Frobenius Side Channel in Factoring: An Abelianization Cap, an Exact Symmetry Wall, and a Frobenius One-Time Pad
description: In the Chebotarev (uniform) model, the Galois/Frobenius side channel on a semiprime N = pq is closed three independent ways. The residue of N carries at most log2[G:G'] bits about anything, every swap-invariant readout carries exactly zero bits about which factor is which, and every readout of the Frobenius of N is exactly independent of every readout of the Frobenius of p, in any finite group.

# The Prime That Keeps Its Secret: Why Galois Symmetry Is a Perfect Cipher Against Factoring

*Every prime number carries a fingerprint — the way it breaks apart inside a number field. Multiply two primes together and you might hope the fingerprints survive. They don't. They are scrambled by a mechanism that is, quite literally, a one-time pad.*

---

## A lock made of two primes

Much of the internet's security still leans on a single wager: that if you multiply two large primes $p$ and $q$ to get $N = pq$, nobody can work backwards from $N$ to $p$ and $q$ in a reasonable amount of time. Over the past half-century, mathematicians have found a handful of genuinely different ways to attack that wager. Broadly, the known methods fall into four families:

1. **Congruences of squares** — find $x$ and $y$ with $x^2 \equiv y^2 \pmod N$, and the greatest common divisor of $x - y$ and $N$ will often expose a factor (the quadratic and number field sieves live here).
2. **Group orders** — work in a group whose size depends secretly on $p$, and wait until an exponent happens to be a multiple of that size (Pollard's $p-1$ method, the elliptic curve method).
3. **Smoothness and index calculus** — collect many numbers that factor into small primes and do linear algebra on the exponents.
4. **Algebraic and complex-multiplication structure** — exploit special arithmetic of curves and number fields attached to $N$.

This article is about a fifth idea, one that sounds as though it ought to work. It belongs to the deepest part of number theory, Galois theory. And it can be shown, in three independent ways, to give an attacker nothing at all.

## Every prime has a fingerprint

Take a polynomial with integer coefficients, say the quartic $f(x) = x^4 - x - 1$. Reduce it modulo a prime $p$. Over the integers mod $p$, $f$ may stay irreducible, or split into a linear factor and an irreducible cubic, or into two quadratics, and so on. The list of degrees of the irreducible pieces is the **splitting type** of $p$. For a quartic, the possible types are
$$1+1+1+1,\quad 1+1+2,\quad 2+2,\quad 1+3,\quad 4.$$

Galois theory explains where these types come from. The roots of $f$ are permuted by a finite group $G$, the **Galois group**. For each prime $p$ (apart from finitely many exceptions) there is a distinguished element of $G$, the **Frobenius element** $\sigma_p$. It is really a whole conjugacy class of elements, which mathematicians call the **Artin symbol**. The splitting type of $p$ is simply the cycle type of $\sigma_p$ as a permutation of the roots. A prime that splits as $1+3$ has a Frobenius that fixes one root and cycles the other three.

How are the Frobenius elements distributed as $p$ varies? The **Chebotarev density theorem**, a far-reaching generalisation of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, answers this. Asymptotically, Frobenius elements are spread *uniformly* over the group: each conjugacy class $C$ is hit by a proportion $|C|/|G|$ of primes. So for the purposes of probability, the right model of "the Frobenius of a random prime" is a uniformly random element of $G$.

So each prime carries a fingerprint, a uniformly random group element that controls how the prime factors in a whole tower of number fields. The tempting idea is this. Suppose we could read off some of the fingerprint of $p$ from $N = pq$ alone. Then we would learn something about $p$, and with enough fingerprints from enough fields we might pin $p$ down.

## What can you actually see from $N$?

The fingerprint of $p$ is hidden, because we don't know $p$. But some of it is visible through $N$. The key fact is the abelian part of Galois theory, class field theory. Every Galois group $G$ has a **derived subgroup** $G'$, generated by all commutators $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$. The quotient $G/G'$, the **abelianization**, is the largest commutative shadow of $G$. By the Kronecker–Weber theorem, the part of the Frobenius that lives in this shadow is determined by **congruences**: the coset $\sigma_p G'$ depends only on $p$ modulo some fixed integer. And because congruences multiply, the coset of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ depends only on $N$ modulo that integer.

That is the side channel. From $N$ you can compute the **residue**, the coset of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ in $G/G'$, and for an Artin-type reader perhaps even the conjugacy class of a product of Frobenius elements. The question is how much this tells you about $p$.

The answer comes in three parts.

## Wall one: the abelian shadow is small

The first barrier is a counting argument, and it is easy to state. **Mutual information**, measured in bits, quantifies how much observing one random quantity tells you about another. If $X$ is a random quantity that can take at most $k$ values, then $X$ can tell you at most $\log_2 k$ bits about *anything*.

The residue takes values in $G/G'$, which has $[G:G']$ elements. By Lagrange's theorem each coset has exactly $|G'|$ elements, so when the Frobenius is uniform the residue is uniform on the cosets, and its entropy is exactly $\log_2[G:G']$. This gives the **Abelianization Cap**:

> **The Abelianization Cap.** For a uniformly random Frobenius $\sigma$ in a finite Galois group $G$, the residue class of $\sigma$ (its coset modulo the derived subgroup) shares at most $\log_2[G:G']$ bits of information with *any* function of $\sigma$ — the splitting type, the conjugacy class, anything. The same bound holds after any further processing of either side.

The second sentence is the **data processing inequality**. You cannot manufacture information by computing with what you already have. Reducing the residue to a smaller modulus, or lumping splitting types together, can only lose bits.

The cap is far smaller than the richness of the fingerprint suggests. Take the symmetric group $S_4$, the Galois group of a "generic" quartic like $x^4 - x - 1$. It has 24 elements and five splitting types. But its derived subgroup is the alternating group $A_4$ of index 2. So **at most one bit** passes from the residue to the splitting type, and that one bit is just the sign of the permutation. Here are the caps for the smallest interesting groups:

| Galois group | order | $[G:G']$ | cap (bits) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $S_3$ | 6 | 2 | 1 |
| $S_4$ | 24 | 2 | 1 |
| $A_4$ | 12 | 3 | $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ |
| $D_4$ | 8 | 4 | 2 |
| $V_4$, $C_4$ | 4 | 4 | 2 |

For a **perfect** group, one equal to its own derived subgroup, the cap is $\log_2 1 = 0$. The icosahedral group $A_5$ is an example. Residues of such fields leak exactly nothing.

The cap is attained precisely when the readout determines the coset. The conjugacy class always does, because cosets of $G'$ are unions of conjugacy classes. The cycle type does for $S_3$ and $S_4$ but not for $A_4$ or $D_4$. In $D_4$, for instance, cycle type yields about $1.656$ of the possible $2$ bits.

## Wall two: the which-factor bit is invisible, exactly

Suppose an attacker could somehow learn the splitting types of both factors, without knowing which type belongs to which prime. There is one bit missing: *is the smaller type carried by $p$ or by $q$?*

Here something stronger than a bound holds. Anything you compute from $N$ alone is symmetric in $p$ and $q$, because $pq = qp$. The residue of $N$ is symmetric too, and so is the conjugacy class of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$. That last fact is less obvious in a non-commutative group, but it follows from the identity
$$\sigma_q\sigma_p = \sigma_p^{-1}(\sigma_p\sigma_q)\,\sigma_p,$$
which says that $\sigma_q\sigma_p$ and $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ are conjugate. Any function that only looks at conjugacy classes therefore cannot tell them apart.

Now comes a beautifully simple principle, the **Symmetry Wall**. Suppose a readout is preserved by a symmetry of the situation, and that symmetry shuffles the possible values of a hidden label transitively. Then the label is perfectly uniform, and the readout tells you *exactly zero* bits about it. Swapping $p$ and $q$ preserves every symmetric readout and flips the which-factor bit, so:

> **The Which-Factor Wall.** In any finite Galois group, abelian or not, consider pairs of Frobenius elements with different splitting types. The bit "which factor carries the smaller type" has entropy exactly $1$. Every readout invariant under exchanging the two factors carries exactly $0$ bits about it. This includes the residue of $N$, the Artin class of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$, and the unordered pair of types.

The zero is exact. It is a statement of symmetry, not a statistical estimate that might creep upward in larger examples. And the bit is genuinely there: an *ordered* readout of types (type of $p$, type of $q$) recovers it in full. The wall extends to numbers with more prime factors. For $N = p_0 p_1\cdots p_m$ with distinct splitting types, the label "which factor carries the smallest type" is worth exactly $\log_2(m+1)$ bits, and every readout symmetric under exchanging two factors leaks exactly none of them.

## Wall three: the Frobenius of $N$ is a one-time pad

The third wall is the most striking one.

Imagine we know nothing about $q$ except that, by Chebotarev, its Frobenius $\sigma_q$ is uniform on the Galois group $G$. Imagine we have narrowed the Frobenius of $p$ down to some set $A$ of candidates, uniform on $A$. And imagine, generously, that we can see the *entire* group element $\sigma_p\sigma_q$, not just its residue.

Does seeing $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ rule out any candidates for $\sigma_p$? The answer is no, and the reason takes one line. Whatever target $\sigma$ we observe and whatever candidate $x \in A$ we consider, the element $y = x^{-1}\sigma$ is a perfectly valid Frobenius for $q$, and $x\cdot y = \sigma$. Every candidate survives. Nothing is pruned, abelian group or not.

In fact the conclusion is stronger than "nothing is pruned". The posterior is *equal* to the prior. The map
$$(x, y) \longmapsto (x,\; xy)$$
is a bijection from $A \times G$ to itself. In cryptographic language this is a shear, and it is exactly the mechanism of a **one-time pad**. In a one-time pad, a message $x$ is combined with a uniformly random key $y$, and the ciphertext $xy$ is uniformly distributed *whatever the message was*. Here the "message" is the Frobenius of $p$ and the "key" is the Frobenius of $q$. Because $\sigma_q$ is uniform on the whole group, the pair $(\sigma_p, \sigma_p\sigma_q)$ is uniform on $A\times G$, so the two coordinates are independent.

> **The Frobenius One-Time Pad.** Let $G$ be any finite group, abelian or not. Let $\sigma_p$ be uniform on a candidate set $A \subseteq G$ and $\sigma_q$ independently uniform on $G$. Then *every* readout of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ — its residue, its conjugacy class, its cycle type, the element itself — carries **exactly zero** bits about *every* readout of $\sigma_p$. Equivalently, after observing any value of the readout, the conditional distribution of $\sigma_p$ equals its prior.

The theorem would be empty if the setup simply had no information to give, so it is worth checking that it doesn't. If we were also shown $\sigma_q$, the pair $(\sigma_p\sigma_q, \sigma_q)$ determines $\sigma_p = (\sigma_p\sigma_q)\sigma_q^{-1}$ and carries the full $\log_2|A|$ bits. The information is there. It is locked away by the cofactor, which acts as the key of the pad.

## Pure synergy: what the residue does know

These walls do not say the residue of $N$ is useless. In $D_4$, a numerical calculation shows that the residue of $N$ carries
$$\frac{39}{16} - \frac34\log_2 3 + \frac{5}{64}\log_2 5 \approx 1.430 \text{ bits}$$
about the *unordered pair* of splitting types of $p$ and $q$. In $S_4$ it carries exactly one bit. What the three walls together say is that *every one of those bits is synergistic*.

- By the one-time pad, the residue of $N$ carries **zero** bits about the splitting type of $p$ alone, and, by the swap symmetry, **zero** bits about that of $q$ alone.
- By the which-factor wall, the ordered pair (type of $p$, type of $q$) carries *exactly the same* information as the unordered pair.
- By the abelianization cap, the total is never more than $\log_2[G:G']$: one bit for $S_4$, two for $D_4$.

So the residue is like two halves of a torn banknote. Neither half is worth anything alone, and the pair, even when it is worth something, never says which half was whose.

## The honest seams

A good impossibility result also says where it stops, and this one has three such places.

**First**, the cap bounds the information carried by the residue, meaning the part of the Frobenius that factors through the abelianization. A readout that does not pass through the abelian shadow is bounded only by the entropy of the splitting type itself. Nothing yet rules out a large non-abelian group combined with some genuinely non-abelian observable computable from $N$. No such observable is known.

**Second**, the which-factor wall assumes symmetry. It applies to every function of $N$, but it does not apply to a side input that treats $p$ and $q$ asymmetrically. Nobody knows how to compute such a side input from $N$ alone.

**Third**, the probabilistic model treats Frobenius elements as exactly uniform and independent. Chebotarev guarantees this in the limit, but the speed of convergence for primes of cryptographic size rests on conjectural refinements, such as effective versions under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

A new attack from this family would therefore need all three at once. It would need a readout of $p$ that does not factor through the abelianization, that breaks the symmetry between $p$ and $q$, and that yields more than a bounded number of bits about which factor is which — all computed from $N$ alone.

## Why it matters

Negative results rarely make headlines, but they are how a field maps its own territory. This one does two things. It identifies the Galois/Frobenius side channel as a genuinely separate fifth family of ideas about factoring. Its mechanism is neither squares, nor group orders, nor smoothness, nor special curves. And it closes that family with three independent arguments: a counting bound (the abelianization cap), an exact symmetry law (the which-factor wall) and an exact independence law (the one-time pad).

Every prime carries an elaborate fingerprint, governed by some of the deepest symmetry in mathematics. But multiplying by an unknown second prime scrambles the fingerprint exactly as a one-time pad scrambles a message, with no residue of the original left over.

# The Galois/Frobenius Side Channel in Integer Factoring: An Abelianization Cap, an Exact Symmetry Wall, and a Frobenius One-Time Pad

**Aristotle**

*2026-10-16*

---

## Abstract

Let $N = pq$ be a product of two unknown primes, and let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a fixed finite Galois extension with group $G$. The Frobenius elements $\sigma_p, \sigma_q \in G$ determine how $p$ and $q$ split in $K$ and in its subfields. Part of the Frobenius of $N$ can be computed from $N$ alone: its image in the abelianization $G/G'$, which by class field theory is determined by a congruence class of $N$. This "Galois/Frobenius side channel" is a candidate attack primitive distinct from the classical families (congruences of squares, group orders, smoothness/index calculus, algebraic/complex-multiplication methods). We model Frobenius elements via the Chebotarev density theorem as uniform random group elements and work in the exact finite Shannon calculus. In this model we show that the channel is closed in three independent ways.

1. **The abelianization cap.** The residue class of a Frobenius element shares at most $\log_2[G:G']$ bits with any readout of it, and this remains true after arbitrary post-processing of either side. For $S_4$ quartic fields, with five splitting types, the cap is one bit. For perfect groups it is zero.
2. **The symmetry wall.** Whenever readout-preserving symmetries act transitively on the values of a hidden label, the label is exactly uniform and the readout carries *exactly* zero bits about it. Consequently, in every finite group, every swap-invariant readout of a semiprime carries exactly $0$ of the $1$ bit that says which factor carries which splitting type. For $m+1$ factors it carries exactly $0$ of $\log_2(m+1)$ bits. The residue of $N$ and every class function of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ are swap-invariant, even in non-abelian groups.
3. **The Frobenius one-time pad.** In any finite group, abelian or not, suppose $\sigma_p$ is uniform on an arbitrary candidate set $A \subseteq G$ and $\sigma_q$ is uniform on $G$. Then every readout of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ is independent of every readout of $\sigma_p$, so the posterior equals the prior. This strengthens the earlier "no pruning" observation, which concerned supports only, to a statement about distributions.

Combining these yields a *semiprime ledger*. The residue of $N$ is uniform on $G/G'$, carries exactly zero bits about the splitting type of either factor alone, carries the same information about the ordered and the unordered pair of types, and never exceeds $\log_2[G:G']$ bits. For $S_4$ it carries exactly $1$ bit about the unordered pair of types; for $D_4$ it carries $\tfrac{39}{16}-\tfrac34\log_2 3+\tfrac{5}{64}\log_2 5 \approx 1.430$ bits. All information in the channel is purely synergistic. We describe the algorithms that evaluate these channels exactly, and we isolate the conjunction of properties that any surviving method in this family must have.

---

## 1. Introduction

The security of RSA-type cryptosystems rests on the presumed hardness of recovering $p$ and $q$ from $N = pq$. Known sub-exponential and special-purpose factoring algorithms fall into four broad families:

- **congruences of squares**: Dixon's method, the quadratic sieve, the number field sieve;
- **group orders**: Pollard's $p-1$, Williams' $p+1$, Lenstra's elliptic curve method;
- **smoothness and index calculus**: relation collection plus linear algebra;
- **algebraic and complex-multiplication structure**: methods exploiting special endomorphism rings or class groups attached to $N$.

A natural fifth idea comes from algebraic number theory. Every prime $p$ unramified in a Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ has a Frobenius conjugacy class in $G = \mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$. That class governs the splitting type of $p$ in every subfield of $K$, which is the factorisation pattern of a defining polynomial modulo $p$. If some of $\sigma_p$ could be read from $N$, then each field $K$ would deliver some bits about $p$. With enough fields, those bits might narrow $p$ down. We call this the **Galois/Frobenius side channel**.

The visible part of the channel is the abelian part. Write $G'$ for the derived subgroup and $G^{\mathrm{ab}} = G/G'$. The fixed field $K^{G'}$ is the maximal abelian subextension. By the Kronecker–Weber theorem it lies in a cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_f)$, and the image of $\sigma_p$ in $G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is a function of $p \bmod f$. Because the Artin map is a homomorphism, the coset $\sigma_p\sigma_q G'$ is a function of $N \bmod f$. We call this coset the **residue** of $N$. It is computable from $N$ without knowing $p$ or $q$.

This paper proves that the side channel yields no usable information, in three independent senses. Section 2 sets up the model. Section 3 proves the **abelianization cap**, together with its extension to all post-processings. Section 4 proves the **independence law** and the **Frobenius one-time pad**. Section 5 proves the abstract **symmetry wall** and derives the **which-factor walls** for two and for many factors. Section 6 assembles the **semiprime ledger** and evaluates it on $S_4$ and $D_4$. Section 7 describes exact algorithms. Section 8 discusses what remains open.

---

## 2. Setting

### 2.1 Finite Shannon calculus

Throughout, a **sample space** is a finite non-empty set $\Omega$ with the uniform probability measure. A **readout** is any function $f : \Omega \to \alpha$ into a set with decidable equality. For $a \in \alpha$, the **fibre** is $\Omega_{f=a} = \{\omega \in \Omega : f(\omega) = a\}$, and
$$\Pr[f = a] = \frac{|\Omega_{f=a}|}{|\Omega|}.$$

**Definition 2.1 (entropy, mutual information).** The (Shannon) **entropy** of $f$ is
$$H(f) = -\sum_{a \in f(\Omega)} \Pr[f=a]\,\log_2 \Pr[f=a].$$
For two readouts $f, g$, the **joint readout** is $(f,g)(\omega) = (f(\omega), g(\omega))$, and the **mutual information** is
$$I(f;g) = H(f) + H(g) - H(f,g).$$
For a third readout $u$, the **conditional mutual information** is
$$I(f;g \mid u) = \sum_{v} \Pr[u=v]\; I_{\Omega_{u=v}}(f;g),$$
where $I_{\Omega_{u=v}}$ is computed on the fibre with its own uniform measure.

We use the following standard facts freely: $0 \le I(f;g) \le \min(H(f), H(g))$; $I(f;g) = I(g;f)$; $H(f) \le \log_2|f(\Omega)|$, with equality iff $f$ is uniform on its image; and the **chain rule** $I(k;(u,w)) = I(k;u) + I(k;w\mid u)$. Mutual information depends only on the partitions of $\Omega$ induced by the readouts, so relabelling the values of a readout injectively does not change it.

### 2.2 The arithmetic model

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be finite Galois with group $G$. Realise $G$ as a permutation group on the $n$ roots of a defining polynomial $F$ of some subfield. For an unramified prime $p$, the factorisation of $F \bmod p$ into irreducibles has degrees equal to the cycle lengths of $\sigma_p$. We call this multiset the **splitting type** $T(\sigma_p)$. More generally, a **type readout** is any function $T : G \to \tau$. The conjugacy class of $\sigma_p$, the **Artin symbol**, is the readout $g \mapsto [g]$.

**Definition 2.2 (coset readout).** Let $N \le G$ be a subgroup. A readout $c : G \to \kappa$ is a **coset readout** for $N$ if for all $g,h \in G$,
$$c(g) = c(h) \iff g^{-1}h \in N.$$
When $N = G'$ we call $c$ the **residue readout**: $c(\sigma_p)$ is the residue class of $p$ in the sense above.

**Modelling assumption (Chebotarev).** By the Chebotarev density theorem, the Frobenius of a random prime is equidistributed in $G$, in the sense that conjugacy class $C$ has density $|C|/|G|$. We model the Frobenius of an unknown prime as a **uniform random element of $G$**, and the Frobenius elements of distinct unknown primes as independent. All theorems below are exact statements in this model. How closely primes of a given size follow the model is a separate, effective-Chebotarev question (Section 8).

For a semiprime, the sample space is $G \times G$, with ordered pairs $(\sigma_p, \sigma_q)$, or a subset of it. The residue of $N$ is the readout $(x,y) \mapsto c(xy)$.

---

## 3. Data processing and the abelianization cap

**Theorem 3.1 (Data processing).** For readouts $f : \Omega \to \alpha$, $g : \Omega \to \beta$ and arbitrary functions $\psi : \alpha \to \gamma$, $\varphi : \beta \to \delta$,
$$I(\psi\circ f;\ \varphi \circ g) \;\le\; I(f;g).$$

*Proof sketch.* It suffices to treat one side, since the other follows by symmetry of $I$. First, $I(g; \psi\circ f) \le I(g; (\psi\circ f, f))$, because adding a coordinate to a readout cannot decrease mutual information; by the chain rule the difference is a conditional mutual information, which is non-negative. Second, $(\psi\circ f, f)$ and $f$ induce the same partition of $\Omega$, since $(\psi(f(\omega)), f(\omega)) = (\psi(f(\omega')), f(\omega'))$ iff $f(\omega)=f(\omega')$. Mutual information depends only on partitions, so $I(g;(\psi\circ f,f)) = I(g;f)$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.2 (Uniform residue).** Let $N \le G$ be finite groups and $c$ a coset readout for $N$. Under the uniform measure on $G$, every fibre of $c$ has exactly $|N|$ elements, and
$$H(c) = \log_2 |c(G)| = \log_2[G:N].$$

*Proof sketch.* The fibre of $c$ through $g$ is the coset $gN$, which has $|N|$ elements (Lagrange). A readout with equal-size fibres is uniform on its image, and its image has $|G|/|N|$ elements. $\square$

**Theorem 3.3 (The abelianization cap).** Let $G$ be a finite group, $G'$ its derived subgroup and $c$ the residue readout. For every type readout $T$ and all post-processings $\psi, \varphi$,
$$I(\psi\circ c;\ \varphi\circ T) \;\le\; I(c;T) \;\le\; \log_2[G:G'] = \log_2|G^{\mathrm{ab}}|.$$

*Proof sketch.* The first inequality is Theorem 3.1. For the second, $I(c;T) \le H(c)$, and $H(c) = \log_2[G:G']$ by Lemma 3.2. $\square$

This covers every coarsening of the residue, for example reduction of $N$ to a smaller modulus or any arithmetic function of the residue class. It also covers every coarsening of the type, for example "is $p$ split completely?" or "does $F$ have a root mod $p$?". None of them can beat $\log_2[G:G']$.

**Corollary 3.4 (Perfect groups leak nothing).** If $G$ is perfect ($G' = G$), then $I(\psi\circ c;\ \varphi\circ T) = 0$ for all $T, \psi, \varphi$.

*Proof sketch.* The cap is $\log_2 1 = 0$, and mutual information is non-negative. $\square$

**Proposition 3.5 (When the cap is attained).** $I(c;T) = \log_2[G:G']$ if and only if the residue is a function of the type on $G$: there is $\phi$ with $c(g) = \phi(T(g))$ for all $g\in G$.

*Proof sketch.* $I(c;T) = H(c) - H(c\mid T)$, and $H(c) = \log_2[G:G']$ by Lemma 3.2. So equality holds iff $H(c\mid T) = 0$, that is, iff $c$ is constant on every fibre of $T$. $\square$

Since $g h g^{-1} h^{-1} \in G'$, every coset of $G'$ is a union of conjugacy classes. Hence the Artin symbol always attains the cap. Table 1 shows exact values for the transitive groups of degree $\le 4$, comparing the quartic or cubic cycle type with the Artin symbol.

**Table 1.** Exact prime-level channel values, in bits, under the uniform model.

| $G$ | $\lvert G\rvert$ | $[G:G']$ | cap $\log_2[G:G']$ | $I(c;\ \text{cycle type})$ | $I(c;\ \text{Artin class})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $S_3$ | 6 | 2 | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $S_4$ | 24 | 2 | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $A_4$ | 12 | 3 | $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ | $\approx 0.918$ | $\log_2 3$ |
| $D_4$ | 8 | 4 | $2$ | $\approx 1.656$ | $2$ |
| $V_4$ | 4 | 4 | $2$ | $\approx 0.811$ | $2$ |
| $C_4$ | 4 | 4 | $2$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |

The cap values are $S_3 = 1$, $S_4 = 1$, $A_4 = \log_2 3$, $D_4 = V_4 = C_4 = 2$. In particular, an $S_4$ quartic field has five splitting types, $1^4$, $1^2 2$, $2^2$, $13$ and $4$. Even so, it transmits at most **one bit** through its residue channel, namely the sign of $\sigma_p$, which is the Legendre-type symbol attached to the discriminant.

---

## 4. The independence law and the Frobenius one-time pad

### 4.1 The independence law

**Lemma 4.1 (Independence law).** Let $f, g$ be readouts on $\Omega$.

(a) *(Probability form.)* If $\Pr[f=a, g=b] = \Pr[f=a]\Pr[g=b]$ for all $a \in f(\Omega)$ and $b \in g(\Omega)$, then $I(f;g) = 0$.

(b) *(Counting form.)* If for all such $a,b$
$$|\Omega_{f=a,\,g=b}|\cdot|\Omega| \;=\; |\Omega_{f=a}|\cdot|\Omega_{g=b}|,$$
then $I(f;g)=0$.

*Proof sketch.* (a) The image of $(f,g)$ lies in $f(\Omega)\times g(\Omega)$. Expand $H(f,g)$ as a double sum over this product and use $\log_2(xy) = \log_2 x + \log_2 y$; the marginal probabilities sum to $1$, so $H(f,g) = H(f) + H(g)$. (b) Divide by $|\Omega|^2$ to obtain (a). $\square$

The counting form makes independence a statement about integers. This is how one verifies exact zeros (Section 7).

### 4.2 The shear

**Lemma 4.2 (Shear count).** Let $G$ be a finite group, $A \subseteq G$, and $P, Q$ predicates on $G$. Then
$$\bigl|\{(x,y) \in A\times G : P(x) \wedge Q(xy)\}\bigr| \;=\; |\{x\in A : P(x)\}|\cdot|\{z\in G: Q(z)\}|.$$

*Proof sketch.* The map $(x,z) \mapsto (x, x^{-1}z)$ sends $\{x\in A: P(x)\}\times\{z\in G : Q(z)\}$ bijectively onto the left-hand set. Its inverse is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$; that both maps land in the right sets uses that $G$ is closed under products and inverses, and that $A \subseteq G$. $\square$

### 4.3 The one-time pad

**Theorem 4.3 (The Frobenius one-time pad).** Let $G$ be a finite group, abelian or not, and let $A\subseteq G$ be any non-empty candidate set. On the sample space $A\times G$, so that $\sigma_p$ is uniform on $A$ and $\sigma_q$ is independently uniform on $G$, let $F$ and $H$ be *arbitrary* readouts of $G$. Then
$$I\bigl(F(\sigma_p);\ H(\sigma_p\sigma_q)\bigr) = 0.$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply Lemma 4.2 three times. With $P = \{F = a\}$ and $Q = \{H = b\}$ it gives the joint cell; with $Q \equiv \mathrm{true}$ it gives the $F$-marginal; with $P\equiv\mathrm{true}$ it gives the $H$-marginal:
$$|\{F=a, H=b\}| = \alpha_a\beta_b,\qquad |\{F = a\}| = \alpha_a|G|,\qquad |\{H=b\}| = |A|\beta_b,$$
where $\alpha_a = |\{x\in A: F(x)=a\}|$ and $\beta_b = |\{z\in G: H(z)=b\}|$. Since $|A\times G| = |A||G|$, the counting form of Lemma 4.1 holds:
$$\alpha_a\beta_b\cdot|A||G| = \alpha_a|G|\cdot|A|\beta_b.\qquad\square$$

The readout $H$ may be the residue of $N$, the Artin symbol of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$, its cycle type, or the element $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ itself. The readout $F$ may be the splitting type of $p$, its residue class, or $\sigma_p$ itself. All channels are exactly zero.

**Corollary 4.4 (Posterior equals prior).** In the setting of Theorem 4.3, for every value $b$ of $H(\sigma_p\sigma_q)$ that occurs and every $a$,
$$\Pr\bigl[F(\sigma_p) = a \;\big|\; H(\sigma_p\sigma_q)=b\bigr] = \Pr\bigl[F(\sigma_p)=a\bigr].$$

*Proof sketch.* The cell counts factor, so the joint probability factors. Dividing by $\Pr[H = b] > 0$ gives the claim. $\square$

**Corollary 4.5 (No pruning).** For any target $\sigma \in G$ and any candidate $x \in A$, there is $y \in G$ with $xy = \sigma$, namely $y = x^{-1}\sigma$. Hence the set of $\sigma_p$ consistent with an observed $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ is all of $A$. Consequently it meets every conjugacy class that $A$ meets, so the Artin channel prunes no candidates.

This support statement was the earlier form of the result, and it settled negatively the conjecture that a non-abelian Artin-symbol channel might give the first residue-type channel with non-trivial pruning. Corollary 4.4 is strictly stronger. Not only does every candidate survive, but the relative weights of the candidates are unchanged.

**Proposition 4.6 (The pad breaks when the cofactor is revealed).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 4.3,
$$I\bigl(\sigma_p;\ (\sigma_p\sigma_q, \sigma_q)\bigr) = \log_2|A|.$$

*Proof sketch.* The pair $(\sigma_p\sigma_q,\sigma_q)$ determines $\sigma_p = (\sigma_p\sigma_q)\sigma_q^{-1}$. So the mutual information equals $H(\sigma_p)$, and $H(\sigma_p) = \log_2|A|$ because each fibre of the first coordinate has exactly $|G|$ elements. $\square$

So the zero of Theorem 4.3 is a genuine independence phenomenon and not an entropy deficit: the information about $\sigma_p$ is present, and $\sigma_q$ acts as its key.

---

## 5. The symmetry wall

### 5.1 The abstract wall

**Definition 5.1 (Label transitivity).** Let $w : \Omega\to\alpha$ (the hidden **label**) and $k:\Omega\to\beta$ (the **readout**) be readouts. We say $w$ is **$k$-label-transitive** if for any two values $a, b \in w(\Omega)$ there is a bijection $\pi : \Omega\to\Omega$ such that

1. $k(\pi\omega) = k(\omega)$ for all $\omega$, so $\pi$ preserves the readout, and
2. $w(\pi\omega) = b \iff w(\omega) = a$, so $\pi$ carries the label class $a$ onto the label class $b$.

**Theorem 5.2 (The symmetry wall).** If $w$ is $k$-label-transitive, then
$$I(w;k) = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad H(w) = \log_2|w(\Omega)|.$$

*Proof sketch.* Fix a readout value $c$ and labels $a,b$, and let $\pi$ be as in Definition 5.1. Then $\pi$ maps the cell $\{w=a, k=c\}$ bijectively onto $\{w=b,k=c\}$, so all cells in a $k$-fibre have the same size. Thus, within each $k$-fibre, the label is uniform on $w(\Omega)$:
$$\Pr[w=a, k=c]\cdot|w(\Omega)| = \Pr[k=c].$$
Summing over $c$ gives $\Pr[w=a]\cdot|w(\Omega)| = 1$, so $w$ is uniform, which is the entropy claim. Combining the two identities gives $\Pr[w=a,k=c]=\Pr[w=a]\Pr[k=c]$, and Lemma 4.1(a) gives $I(w;k)=0$. $\square$

The zero here is **exact**; it is a consequence of symmetry, not an estimate.

### 5.2 Swap invariance of Galois readouts of $N$

**Definition 5.3.** A readout $H : G\to\kappa$ is a **class function** if $H(ghg^{-1}) = H(h)$ for all $g,h\in G$.

**Proposition 5.4 (The residue is a class function).** Every residue readout $c$ (a coset readout for $G'$) is a class function.

*Proof sketch.* $(ghg^{-1})^{-1}h$ is a commutator $g h^{-1} g^{-1} h$, so it lies in $G'$. $\square$

**Proposition 5.5 (Class functions of the product are swap-invariant).** If $H$ is a class function, then $H(yx) = H(xy)$ for all $x,y\in G$.

*Proof sketch.* $yx = x^{-1}(xy)x$. $\square$

Thus the residue of $N$, the Artin symbol of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ and the cycle type of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ are all symmetric under $p\leftrightarrow q$, even when $G$ is non-abelian. Any readout that is a function of $N$ is symmetric in the same way.

### 5.3 The which-factor wall

Let $T : G\to\tau$ be a type readout into a totally ordered set, and let $A \subseteq G$. Define the **asymmetric pair space**
$$\Omega_{A,T} = \{(x,y)\in A\times A : T(x)\neq T(y)\}$$
and the **which-factor bit** $b(x,y) = [\,T(x) < T(y)\,]$: does the first factor carry the smaller type?

**Theorem 5.6 (The which-factor wall).** Let $G$ be any group and $A\subseteq G$ any finite set. Let $k$ be any readout of $\Omega_{A,T}$ with $k(y,x) = k(x,y)$. Then
$$I(b;k) = 0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad H(b) = 1 \text{ whenever } \Omega_{A,T}\neq\varnothing.$$

*Proof sketch.* The swap $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$ is an involution of $\Omega_{A,T}$. It preserves $k$, and it flips $b$ because the types are distinct. Hence $b$ is $k$-label-transitive and Theorem 5.2 applies. Both values of $b$ occur when the space is non-empty, so $H(b) = \log_2 2 = 1$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.7 (Residue and Artin readouts hide the bit).** For a finite group $G$, a residue readout $c$ and a class function $H$, the readouts
$$\bigl(c(xy),\ \min(T x, T y),\ \max(T x,T y)\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(H(xy),\ \min(Tx,Ty),\ \max(Tx,Ty)\bigr)$$
both carry exactly zero bits about $b$ on $\Omega_{G,T}$. So even an adversary who knows the residue of $N$ (or the Artin class of its Frobenius) *and* the unordered pair of splitting types learns nothing about which factor is which.

*Proof sketch.* By Propositions 5.4–5.5 these readouts are swap-invariant. Apply Theorem 5.6. $\square$

**Proposition 5.8 (Non-vacuity).** The ordered readout $(T x, T y)$ satisfies $I(b;(Tx,Ty)) = H(b)$.

*Proof sketch.* $b$ is a function of $(Tx,Ty)$. $\square$

### 5.4 The multi-prime wall

For $N = p_0p_1\cdots p_m$, let
$$\Omega^{(m)}_{A,T} = \{x\in A^{m+1} : i\mapsto T(x_i) \text{ is injective}\}$$
be the tuples of candidate Frobenius elements with pairwise distinct types. The label $\mu(x)$ is the index $i$ at which $T(x_i)$ is smallest.

**Theorem 5.9 (The multi-prime wall).** Let $k$ be a readout of $\Omega^{(m)}_{A,T}$ that is invariant under exchanging any two coordinates. Then
$$I(\mu;k) = 0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad H(\mu) = \log_2(m+1)\text{ whenever }\Omega^{(m)}_{A,T}\neq\varnothing.$$

*Proof sketch.* Permuting coordinates by a permutation $s$ moves the minimal-type index $i$ to $s^{-1}(i)$. The transposition $(i\,j)$ preserves $k$ and the space, and carries the label class $i$ onto the label class $j$. So $\mu$ is $k$-label-transitive; Theorem 5.2 gives $I = 0$, and all $m+1$ indices occur. $\square$

Examples of admissible $k$ are the image of $\sigma_{p_0}\cdots\sigma_{p_m}$ in an abelian quotient, the multiset of splitting types, and any symmetric function of the factors. As in Proposition 5.8, the ordered tuple of types recovers the full $\log_2(m+1)$ bits.

---

## 6. The semiprime ledger

Now take the full semiprime sample space $G\times G$, so that $(\sigma_p,\sigma_q)$ is uniform, and the residue of $N$, $\rho(x,y) = c(xy)$.

**Theorem 6.1 (The residue of $N$ is uniform).** $H(\rho) = \log_2[G:G']$.

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 4.2 with $A = G$, the fibre $\{c(xy) = c(g)\}$ has $|G|\cdot|gG'| = |G|\,|G'|$ elements. All fibres are equal, and the image of $\rho$ equals the image of $c$, which has $[G:G']$ elements. $\square$

**Theorem 6.2 (The semiprime abelianization cap).** For every readout $R$ of the ordered pair $(\sigma_p,\sigma_q)$,
$$I(\rho;R) \le \log_2[G:G'].$$

*Proof sketch.* $I(\rho;R)\le H(\rho)$, and $H(\rho) = \log_2[G:G']$ by Theorem 6.1. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (Pure synergy: the residue is blind to each factor).** For every readout $F$ of a single Frobenius element,
$$I\bigl(\rho;\ F(\sigma_p)\bigr) = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad I\bigl(\rho;\ F(\sigma_q)\bigr)=0.$$

*Proof sketch.* The first is Theorem 4.3 with $A = G$ and $H = c$. For the second, apply the swap bijection of $G\times G$. It exchanges $F(\sigma_p)$ and $F(\sigma_q)$, and it preserves $\rho$ by Propositions 5.4–5.5, since $c(yx)=c(xy)$. Mutual information is invariant under bijections of the sample space, so the second channel equals the first. $\square$

**Theorem 6.4 (Ordered equals unordered).** Let $\Omega_0\subseteq G\times G$ be closed under the swap, let $k$ be a swap-invariant readout on $\Omega_0$, and let $T$ be any type readout into a totally ordered set. Then
$$I\bigl(k;\ (T\sigma_p, T\sigma_q)\bigr) \;=\; I\bigl(k;\ \{T\sigma_p, T\sigma_q\}\bigr),$$
where $\{T\sigma_p, T\sigma_q\}$ denotes the unordered pair $(\min,\max)$.

*Proof sketch.* The ordered pair induces the same partition as (unordered pair, which-factor bit). By the chain rule,
$$I(k;\text{ordered}) = I(k;\text{unordered}) + I(k;\, b\mid\text{unordered}).$$
Fix a fibre $\{T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q\} = \{s_1,s_2\}$. If $s_1 = s_2$, the bit is constant on the fibre and the conditional term vanishes. If $s_1 < s_2$, the fibre is swap-closed, every element has distinct types, and the swap preserves $k$ and flips $b$. Theorem 5.2 on the fibre then gives zero. $\square$

**Corollary 6.5 (The residue never learns which factor is which).** For every finite group $G$, every class function $H$ (the residue of $N$, the Artin symbol, the cycle type of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$, …) and every type readout $T$,
$$I\bigl(H(\sigma_p\sigma_q);\ (T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q)\bigr) = I\bigl(H(\sigma_p\sigma_q);\ \{T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q\}\bigr).$$

This proves, uniformly and without evaluating any entropy, the equality of ordered and unordered channels that was previously checked case by case for $S_3, S_4, A_4, D_4, V_4, C_4$.

### 6.1 Two worked fields

**Theorem 6.6 ($S_4$: pure synergy in a five-type field).** Let $G = S_4$ act on four roots, $T$ the cycle type and $c$ the sign coset. On $S_4\times S_4$:
$$I(\rho;T\sigma_p) = 0,\quad I(\rho;T\sigma_q)=0,\quad I\bigl(\rho;\{T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q\}\bigr) = 1,\quad I(\rho;R)\le 1 \ \text{ for every readout } R.$$

**Theorem 6.7 ($D_4$: pure synergy above the binary ceiling).** Let $G = D_4\le S_4$ (order $8$, $G'$ the centre of order $2$), $T$ the quartic cycle type and $c$ the coset readout of $G'$. On $D_4\times D_4$:
$$I(\rho;T\sigma_p) = I(\rho;T\sigma_q) = 0,\qquad I\bigl(\rho;\{T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q\}\bigr) = \frac{39}{16} - \frac34\log_2 3 + \frac{5}{64}\log_2 5 \approx 1.430 > 1,$$
and $I(\rho;R) \le 2$ for every readout $R$.

*Proof sketch of 6.6–6.7.* The zeros are Theorem 6.3. The caps are Theorem 6.2 with $[S_4:A_4] = 2$ and $[D_4 : Z(D_4)] = 4$. The middle values are exact finite computations. Each requires the joint distribution of the residue and the unordered type pair over $576$ pairs (for $S_4$) or $64$ pairs (for $D_4$). For $D_4$ the inequality $>1$ uses $\log_2 3 < 2$ and $\log_2 5 > 2$. $\square$

The ledger can be summarised as follows. Every bit that the residue of $N$ reveals about the shape of the factorisation is **synergistic**: it is invisible to any reader of one factor, it says nothing about which factor carries which type, and in total it is at most $\log_2[G:G']$.

---

## 7. Algorithms

All quantities in this paper are exact functions of finite multisets of integers, and they can be evaluated exactly.

### 7.1 Exact channel evaluation

*Input:* a finite sample space $\Omega$ (listed explicitly) and readouts $f,g$.
1. Tabulate the counters $n_f(a) = |\Omega_{f=a}|$, $n_g(b)$ and $n_{fg}(a,b)$ in one pass.
2. Compute $H(f) = \log_2|\Omega| - \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_a n_f(a)\log_2 n_f(a)$, and similarly $H(g)$ and $H(f,g)$.
3. Return $I = H(f)+H(g)-H(f,g)$.
4. *(Exact zero certificate.)* Check the integer identities $n_{fg}(a,b)\,|\Omega| = n_f(a)\,n_g(b)$ for all $a,b$. If all hold, then $I = 0$ exactly (Lemma 4.1(b)).

The cost is $O(|\Omega|)$ hash operations plus $O(|f(\Omega)|\cdot|g(\Omega)|)$ for the certificate.

### 7.2 Abelianization cap

*Input:* generators of a permutation group $G$.
1. Enumerate $G$ by breadth-first closure under the generators.
2. Generate $G'$ from all commutators $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$, again by closure.
3. Represent the residue readout by $c(g) = \min_{n\in G'} gn$, the lexicographically least element of $gG'$.
4. Return $\log_2(|G|/|G'|)$. Optionally evaluate $I(c;T)$ via 7.1 and test attainment via Proposition 3.5: is $c$ constant on the fibres of $T$?

For the small groups of interest this is instantaneous. For permutation groups in general, Schreier–Sims methods compute $|G|$ and $|G'|$ in polynomial time without enumeration.

### 7.3 Symmetry-wall certificate

*Input:* $\Omega$, label $w$, readout $k$, and a finite set $\Pi$ of candidate bijections of $\Omega$ (for example coordinate transpositions).
1. Keep the $\pi\in\Pi$ that map $\Omega$ to itself and preserve $k$.
2. Build the graph on $w(\Omega)$ with an edge $a \to b$ whenever some kept $\pi$ maps the class $w^{-1}(a)$ onto $w^{-1}(b)$.
3. If this graph is complete (every ordered pair is joined), conclude $I(w;k)=0$ and $H(w) = \log_2|w(\Omega)|$ by Theorem 5.2.

This certifies exact zeros without computing a single logarithm. It is how the which-factor and multi-prime walls generalise from finite tables to all groups.

### 7.4 Representative numbers

The following were obtained by direct enumeration with the procedures above, in the uniform model.

- **Pad.** In $S_4$, for random candidate sets $A$ with $|A|\in[2,9]$, the channels between {type of $\sigma_p$, $\sigma_p$} and {type, Artin class, residue, element} of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ are all exactly zero, with every cell-count identity holding. Revealing $\sigma_q$ yields exactly $\log_2|A|$ bits.
- **Which-factor.** For $S_3, S_4, A_4, D_4$: $H(b) = 1$; residue + unordered types gives $0$; Artin + unordered types gives $0$; ordered types gives $1$.
- **Multi-prime.** In $S_4$ with $3$ factors ($5256$ tuples with distinct types), the label has $\log_2 3$ bits and the residue together with the multiset of types gives $0$.

---

## 8. Discussion

### 8.1 A fifth primitive, closed

The Galois/Frobenius side channel is structurally distinct from the four classical families. It uses neither quadratic relations, nor group orders, nor smoothness, nor special endomorphisms; it reads the splitting behaviour of the hidden factors. The results above close it in three logically independent ways:

| closure | type of statement | mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Abelianization cap | upper bound | Lagrange: the residue is uniform on $[G:G']$ cosets |
| Which-factor / multi-prime wall | exact zero | label-transitive symmetry ($pq = qp$) |
| Frobenius one-time pad | exact independence | shear bijection $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$ |

The cap limits *how much* any residue can say. The wall shows that the residue cannot say *which* factor is which. The pad shows that the full Frobenius of $N$ says nothing about the Frobenius of $p$ alone.

### 8.2 The seams

The closures have precise boundaries.

1. **The cap bounds the residue content, not the full type.** A readout that does not factor through the abelianization coset is bounded only by $H(T)$. A large non-abelian group with large $\log_2[G:G']$ *and* a positive gap between the ordered and unordered channels is not excluded in principle. Note, however, that Theorem 6.4 forbids such a gap for every swap-invariant readout.
2. **The wall's hypothesis is symmetry.** Every wall statement assumes the readout is swap-invariant, which every function of $N$ is. A readout of an *asymmetric side input* is untouched, but no such side input computable from $N$ is known.
3. **Distributional assumptions.** The model takes Frobenius elements to be exactly uniform and independent. For primes of a fixed large size this is an effective Chebotarev statement. Explicit error terms are known under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis but are conjectural in general. The theorems are exact *in the model*, and transfer to actual primes only up to such error terms.

Accordingly, any new method in this family must, as a **conjunction**, supply a readout of $p$ that

- (i) does not factor through $G^{\mathrm{ab}}$,
- (ii) breaks the $p\leftrightarrow q$ symmetry, and
- (iii) yields more than $O(1)$ bits about which factor is which,

all computed from $N$ alone. By the one-time pad, condition (i) is not enough by itself: even the full non-abelian Frobenius of $N$ is independent of that of $p$.

### 8.3 Relation to the classical picture

The pad has a simple arithmetic shadow. When $G = (\mathbb{Z}/f\mathbb{Z})^\times$, the residue of $N$ is $N \bmod f$. Knowing $N \bmod f$ tells you nothing about $p \bmod f$ when $q \bmod f$ is uniform on the units, because multiplication by a uniform unit is a one-time pad. Theorem 4.3 says this familiar fact survives verbatim in every finite group, for every readout and every candidate set.

---

## 9. Future directions

1. **Multi-prime one-time pad with an abelian product readout.** For $N = p_1\cdots p_k$ with Frobenius elements i.i.d. uniform on $G$, the coset of $\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_k$ in $G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ should share exactly zero bits with every readout of any $k-1$ of the factors, and at most $\log_2[G:G']$ bits with any readout of all $k$. The shear $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\mapsto(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1},x_1\cdots x_k)$ is a bijection, so the pad should iterate by induction using Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.1(b).
2. **Semiprime completeness criterion.** For $(\sigma_p,\sigma_q)$ uniform on $G\times G$, conjecturally $I\bigl(c(\sigma_p\sigma_q);\{T\sigma_p,T\sigma_q\}\bigr) = \log_2[G:G']$ if and only if $T$ determines the abelianization coset, that is, $c = \phi\circ T$ on $G$. One direction follows from Theorem 6.4: if $c = \phi\circ T$, the residue of $N$ is a function of the ordered pair of cosets, and Theorem 6.4 transfers this to the unordered pair. The converse needs a fibrewise analysis of equality in $I\le H$. The values in Section 6 are consistent with the conjecture: $S_3$ and $S_4$ attain the cap, where the cycle type determines the sign, while $D_4$ ($\approx 1.430 < 2$) and $A_4$ fall short, where it does not.
3. **Effective transfer.** Quantify, under GRH-type effective Chebotarev bounds, the deviation of the true channel on primes of size $X$ from the model values. The aim is to show that the exact zeros become $o(1)$ uniformly in the readout.
4. **Beyond the abelianization.** Characterise the readouts that are not class functions of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ yet are computable from $N$. Determine whether any of them can break condition (ii).

The Galois/Frobenius side channel: numerical demonstrations.

Every quantity below is an *exact* Shannon quantity on a finite, uniformly weighted
sample space (a finite Galois group, or a product of copies of it).  Groups are
realised as permutation groups, so the "splitting type" of a prime is the cycle
type of its Frobenius element acting on the roots of a defining polynomial.

Sections
  1. The abelianization cap      I(residue ; type) <= log2 [G : G']
  2. Data processing             post-processing never increases a channel
  3. The Frobenius one-time pad  readouts of sigma_p sigma_q say nothing about sigma_p
  4. Posterior = prior, and the pad breaking once the cofactor is revealed
  5. The which-factor wall       exactly one hidden bit, exactly zero leaked
  6. The multi-prime wall        log2(m+1) hidden bits, zero leaked
  7. The semiprime ledger        pure synergy in the S4 and D4 quartic fields

Run:  python3 demo.py

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import permutations, product
from math import log2
from typing import Callable, Dict, Hashable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple, TypeVar

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]
T = TypeVar("T")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Permutation groups
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def mul(a: Perm, b: Perm) -> Perm:
    """Composition a o b (apply b first)."""
    return tuple(a[b[i]] for i in range(len(b)))


def inv(a: Perm) -> Perm:
    r = [0] * len(a)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        r[x] = i
    return tuple(r)


def identity(n: int) -> Perm:
    return tuple(range(n))


def generate(gens: Sequence[Perm]) -> Set[Perm]:
    """Subgroup generated by gens (closure under right multiplication)."""
    e = identity(len(gens[0]))
    group: Set[Perm] = {e}
    frontier: List[Perm] = [e]
    while frontier:
        new: List[Perm] = []
        for x in frontier:
            for g in gens:
                y = mul(x, g)
                if y not in group:
                    group.add(y)
                    new.append(y)
        frontier = new
    return group


def derived_subgroup(G: Set[Perm]) -> Set[Perm]:
    n = len(next(iter(G)))
    comms = [mul(mul(a, b), mul(inv(a), inv(b))) for a in G for b in G]
    return generate(comms) if comms else {identity(n)}


def cycle_type(p: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Splitting type of a prime with Frobenius p: the multiset of cycle lengths."""
    seen: Set[int] = set()
    lengths: List[int] = []
    for i in range(len(p)):
        if i in seen:
            continue
        j, length = i, 0
        while j not in seen:
            seen.add(j)
            j = p[j]
            length += 1
        lengths.append(length)
    return tuple(sorted(lengths))


def coset_readout(N: Set[Perm]) -> Callable[[Perm], Perm]:

    assert all(mul(p, mul(inv(p), sigma)) == sigma for p in elems)
    print(f"  No pruning: for a fixed target sigma_N, every p has the compensating q = p^-1 sigma"
          f" ({len(compensators)} of {len(elems)} candidates survive).\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The which-factor wall
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_which_factor() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5. THE WHICH-FACTOR WALL   H(bit) = 1 and I(bit ; k) = 0 for swap-invariant k")
    print("=" * 78)
    for name in ["S3", "S4", "D4", "A4"]:
        G = GROUPS[name]
        elems = sorted(G)
        space = [(x, y) for x in elems for y in elems if cycle_type(x) != cycle_type(y)]
        bit = lambda z: cycle_type(z[0]) < cycle_type(z[1])
        c = coset_readout(derived_subgroup(G))
        cls = conj_class_readout(G)
        k_res = lambda z: (c(mul(z[0], z[1])), min(cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])),
                           max(cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])))
        k_art = lambda z: (cls(mul(z[0], z[1])), min(cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])),
                           max(cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])))
        h = entropy([bit(z) for z in space])
        i_res = mutual_info(space, bit, k_res)
        i_art = mutual_info(space, bit, k_art)
        i_ord = mutual_info(space, bit, lambda z: (cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])))
        assert abs(h - 1) < 1e-12 and abs(i_res) < 1e-12 and abs(i_art) < 1e-12
        print(f"  {name}: H(bit)={fmt(h)}  I(bit; residue+unordered types)={fmt(i_res)}"
              f"  I(bit; Artin+unordered)={fmt(i_art)}  I(bit; ORDERED types)={fmt(i_ord)}")
    print("  The zero is exact, and the ordered readout shows the bit is really there.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The multi-prime wall
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_multi_prime() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6. THE MULTI-PRIME WALL   N = p0 p1 ... pm,  H(label) = log2(m+1),  I = 0")
    print("=" * 78)
    G = S4
    elems = sorted(G)
    c = coset_readout(derived_subgroup(G))
    for m in [1, 2]:
        space = [x for x in product(elems, repeat=m + 1)
                 if len({cycle_type(g) for g in x}) == m + 1]
        label = lambda x: min(range(m + 1), key=lambda i: cycle_type(x[i]))

        def k_sym(x: Tuple[Perm, ...]) -> Hashable:
            prod_coset = c(x[0])
            for g in x[1:]:
                prod_coset = c(mul(prod_coset, g))
            return (prod_coset, tuple(sorted(cycle_type(g) for g in x)))

        h = entropy([label(x) for x in space])
        i0 = mutual_info(space, label, k_sym)
        i_ord = mutual_info(space, label, lambda x: tuple(cycle_type(g) for g in x))
        assert abs(h - log2(m + 1)) < 1e-12 and abs(i0) < 1e-12
        print(f"  m+1={m+1} factors, |space|={len(space)}: H(label)={fmt(h)} = log2({m+1});"
              f" I(label; residue+multiset of types)={fmt(i0)}; ordered={fmt(i_ord)}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The semiprime ledger
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_ledger() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7. THE SEMIPRIME LEDGER: PURE SYNERGY")
    print("=" * 78)
    for name in ["S4", "D4"]:
        G = GROUPS[name]
        elems = sorted(G)
        space = [(x, y) for x in elems for y in elems]
        c = coset_readout(derived_subgroup(G))
        res = lambda z: c(mul(z[0], z[1]))
        h_res = entropy([res(z) for z in space])
        i_p = mutual_info(space, res, lambda z: cycle_type(z[0]))
        i_q = mutual_info(space, res, lambda z: cycle_type(z[1]))
        i_uno = mutual_info(space, res, lambda z: tuple(sorted([cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])])))
        i_ord = mutual_info(space, res, lambda z: (cycle_type(z[0]), cycle_type(z[1])))
        print(f"  {name}: H(residue of N)={fmt(h_res)} = log2[G:G']")
        print(f"      I(res ; type p)={fmt(i_p)}  I(res ; type q)={fmt(i_q)}"
              f"  I(res ; {{Tp,Tq}})={fmt(i_uno)}  I(res ; (Tp,Tq))={fmt(i_ord)}")
        assert abs(i_p) < 1e-12 and abs(i_q) < 1e-12 and abs(i_uno - i_ord) < 1e-12
    closed = 39 / 16 - 0.75 * log2(3) + 5 / 64 * log2(5)
    print(f"  D4 closed form 39/16 - (3/4)log2 3 + (5/64)log2 5 = {fmt(closed)}  (> 1, <= 2)")
    print("  Zero bits about each factor alone, yet positive bits about the pair:")
    print("  every bit the residue of N leaks is synergistic, and ordered = unordered.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_cap()

algorithms.name: Exact Mutual Information with an Integer Certificate of Independence
algorithms.description: Evaluates I(f;g) = H(f) + H(g) - H(f,g) exactly on a finite, uniformly weighted sample space by a single counting pass, and certifies an exact zero by checking the integer identities #{f=a,g=b}·|Ω| = #{f=a}·#{g=b} for every cell (the counting form of the independence law). The certificate avoids any floating-point judgment: it is a finite set of integer equalities that imply independence. Complexity O(|Ω|) hash operations plus O(|f(Ω)|·|g(Ω)|) for the certificate. This is the workhorse behind every exact zero in the theory: the one-time pad, the which-factor wall, and the pure-synergy statements.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: finite list Ω, readouts f, g
1. cf, cg, cfg ← empty counters
2. FOR ω in Ω: a ← f(ω); b ← g(ω); cf[a]++, cg[b]++, cfg[(a,b)]++
3. H(X) ← log2|Ω| − (1/|Ω|) Σ_x c_X(x) log2 c_X(x)   for X ∈ {f, g, (f,g)}
4. I ← H(f) + H(g) − H(f,g)
5. certified ← ∀ a ∈ keys(cf), b ∈ keys(cg): cfg[(a,b)]·|Ω| = cf[a]·cg[b]
6. RETURN (I, certified)      // certified ⇒ I = 0 exactly
algorithms.code:
"""Exact mutual information on a finite uniform sample space, with an integer
certificate for exact independence (the counting form of the independence law)."""
from collections import Counter
from math import log2
from typing import Callable, Hashable, Sequence, Tuple, TypeVar

W = TypeVar("W")


def entropy_from_counts(counts: Counter, n: int) -> float:
    # H = log2 n - (1/n) * sum_a c_a log2 c_a   (numerically stable form)
    return log2(n) - sum(c * log2(c) for c in counts.values()) / n


def exact_channel(space: Sequence[W],
                  f: Callable[[W], Hashable],
                  g: Callable[[W], Hashable]) -> Tuple[float, bool]:
    """Return (I(f;g), certified_zero).

    certified_zero is True iff every cell satisfies the integer identity
    #{f=a, g=b} * |space| == #{f=a} * #{g=b}, which proves I(f;g) = 0 exactly."""
    n = len(space)
    cf: Counter = Counter()
    cg: Counter = Counter()
    cfg: Counter = Counter()
    for w in space:
        a, b = f(w), g(w)
        cf[a] += 1
        cg[b] += 1
        cfg[(a, b)] += 1
    mi = entropy_from_counts(cf, n) + entropy_from_counts(cg, n) - entropy_from_counts(cfg, n)
    certified = all(cfg.get((a, b), 0) * n == cf[a] * cg[b] for a in cf for b in cg)
    return mi, certified


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Z/7^* one-time pad: residue of N = p*q mod 7 vs residue of p mod 7.
    units = list(range(1, 7))
    space = [(p, q) for p in units for q in units]
    print(exact_channel(space, lambda z: z[0], lambda z: (z[0] * z[1]) % 7))   # (0.0, True)
    print(exact_channel(space, lambda z: z[0], lambda z: ((z[0] * z[1]) % 7, z[1])))  # log2 6

algorithms.name: Computation of the Abelianization Cap log2[G:G'] and Its Attainment Test
algorithms.description: Given generators of a permutation group G (the Galois group acting on roots), enumerates G by breadth-first closure, generates the derived subgroup G' from all commutators aba⁻¹b⁻¹, and realises the residue readout as the lexicographically least element of each coset gG'. Returns the cap log2[G:G'] (the maximal number of bits any residue readout can carry about any type readout), the actual channel I(c;T) for a chosen type readout T, and whether the cap is attained, which happens iff the residue is constant on every fibre of T. Brute-force cost is O(|G|²) for the commutators plus O(|G|·|G'|) for the coset readout; for large groups Schreier–Sims methods give |G| and |G'| in polynomial time.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: generators S of a permutation group; type readout T
1. G ← closure(S)
2. D ← closure({a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ : a, b ∈ G})          // derived subgroup G'
3. c(g) ← min_{n ∈ D} g·n                         // coset readout
4. cap ← log2(|G| / |D|)
5. I ← MutualInformation(G, c, T)
6. attained ← ∀ t: |{c(g) : T(g) = t}| = 1
7. RETURN (|G|, [G:G'], cap, I, attained)

algorithms.name: Symmetry-Wall Certificate via Readout-Preserving Label-Transitive Bijections
algorithms.description: Certifies I(label; readout) = 0 and H(label) = log2(#labels) exactly, without computing a logarithm. It keeps those candidate bijections of the sample space that preserve the readout, and checks that for every ordered pair of label values (a, b) some kept bijection maps the label class of a exactly onto the label class of b. By the symmetry wall theorem, this transitivity forces the label to be uniform inside every readout fibre, so the joint law factors. Swapping the two factors of a semiprime certifies the which-factor wall, and coordinate transpositions certify the multi-prime wall. Cost O(|Π|·|Ω| + L²·|Π|·|Ω|) for |Π| moves and L labels.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: Ω, label w, readout k, candidate bijections Π
1. Good ← {π ∈ Π : π(Ω) = Ω bijectively and k∘π = k on Ω}
2. FOR each ordered pair (a, b) of label values:
3.     reach(a,b) ← (a = b) OR ∃ π ∈ Good: π(w⁻¹(a)) = w⁻¹(b)
4. IF all reach(a,b): RETURN 'I(w;k) = 0 and H(w) = log2 #labels'
5. ELSE RETURN 'no certificate'

visualizations.description: Grouped bar chart over S3, S4, A4, D4, V4 and C4: the cap log2[G:G'], the residue channel through the Artin class (which always attains the cap), and the residue channel through the cycle type (which attains it only for S3 and S4). The chart shows that an S4 field with five splitting types still transmits at most one bit.
visualizations.code:
"""Bar chart: the abelianization cap log2[G:G'] versus the residue channel achieved by the
cycle type and by the Artin class, for the transitive groups of degree <= 4."""
from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations
from math import log2
from typing import Callable, Hashable, List, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]
mul = lambda a, b: tuple(a[i] for i in b)


def inv(a: Perm) -> Perm:
    r = [0] * len(a)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        r[x] = i
    return tuple(r)


def closure(gens: List[Perm]) -> Set[Perm]:
    e = tuple(range(len(gens[0]))); S = {e}; fr = [e]
    while fr:
        nx = []
        for x in fr:
            for g in gens:
                y = mul(x, g)
                if y not in S:
                    S.add(y); nx.append(y)
        fr = nx
    return S


def ctype(p: Perm) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    seen, out = set(), []
    for i in range(len(p)):
        if i not in seen:
            j, l = i, 0
            while j not in seen:
                seen.add(j); j = p[j]; l += 1
            out.append(l)
    return tuple(sorted(out))


def MI(space: List[Perm], f: Callable[[Perm], Hashable], g: Callable[[Perm], Hashable]) -> float:
    H = lambda xs: -sum(c / len(xs) * log2(c / len(xs)) for c in Counter(xs).values())
    a = [f(w) for w in space]; b = [g(w) for w in space]
    return H(a) + H(b) - H(list(zip(a, b)))


groups = {"S3": closure([(1, 0, 2), (1, 2, 0)]), "S4": set(permutations(range(4))),
          "A4": closure([(1, 2, 0, 3), (0, 2, 3, 1)]), "D4": closure([(1, 2, 3, 0), (2, 1, 0, 3)]),
          "V4": closure([(1, 0, 3, 2), (2, 3, 0, 1)]), "C4": closure([(1, 2, 3, 0)])}
names, caps, ict, icl = [], [], [], []
for name, G in groups.items():
    D = closure([mul(mul(a, b), mul(inv(a), inv(b))) for a in G for b in G])
    c = lambda g, D=D: min(mul(g, n) for n in D)
    cls = lambda g, G=G: min(mul(mul(h, g), inv(h)) for h in G)
    sp = sorted(G)
    names.append(name); caps.append(log2(len(G) // len(D)))
    ict.append(MI(sp, c, ctype)); icl.append(MI(sp, c, cls))

x = range(len(names)); w = 0.27
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.bar([i - w for i in x], caps, w, label="cap  log2[G:G']", color="#f2b134")
ax.bar(list(x), icl, w, label="I(residue ; Artin class)", color="#4cb07a")
ax.bar([i + w for i in x], ict, w, label="I(residue ; cycle type)", color="#3c8ddc")
ax.set_xticks(list(x)); ax.set_xticklabels(names); ax.set_ylabel("bits")
ax.set_title("The abelianization cap: no residue readout beats log2[G:G']")
ax.legend(); fig.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("abelianization_cap.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

interactive_layout:
# The Prime That Keeps Its Secret *An interactive tour of the Galois/Frobenius side channel and the three ways it is closed.* Suppose someone hands you $N = pq$. Every prime carries a **Frobenius element** $\sigma_p$ in the Galois group $G$ of a number field. This element is a fingerprint that dictates how $p$ factors in that field. Part of the fingerprint of $N$ is visible from $N$ alone. Can it betray $p$? This page walks through three answers, each sharper than the last: a **cap**, a **wall**, and a **one-time pad**. Every number on the page is computed exactly; nothing is sampled.
Background: Frobenius elements, splitting types, and Chebotarev (click to expand) Take a polynomial $F$ with Galois group $G$, acting on its roots. For an unramified prime $p$, reduce $F$ modulo $p$. The degrees of the irreducible factors equal the cycle lengths of the Frobenius $\sigma_p$, viewed as a permutation of the roots; this pattern is the **splitting type** of $p$. For $F = x^4 - x - 1$ (group $S_4$), the types are $1+1+1+1$, $1+1+2$, $2+2$, $1+3$ and $4$. The [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem) says that Frobenius elements are equidistributed: a conjugacy class $C$ is hit by a proportion $|C|/|G|$ of primes. So we model the Frobenius of an unknown prime as a **uniform random element of $G$**, independent across primes. The part visible from $N$ is the image of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ in the [abelianization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutator_subgroup) $G/G'$. By the [Kronecker–Weber theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%E2%80%93Weber_theorem) this image is determined by a congruence class of $N$. We call it the **residue of $N$**.
Information is measured by [mutual information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_information): $I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y)$, in bits, where $H$ is Shannon entropy. --- ## 1. The laboratory Start by playing. Choose a Galois group and a set $A$ of candidates for $\sigma_p$. Then pick any readout of $\sigma_p$ and any readout of $\sigma_N = \sigma_p\sigma_q$. Whatever you choose, the number stays at **zero**. {{interactive_demo:0}} Things to try: - Choose $S_4$, click **one splitting type**, and set the readout of $\sigma_N$ to *the element itself*. You see the whole non-abelian Frobenius of $N$, and you still learn nothing about $\sigma_p$. - Press **Reveal σ_q as well**. The channel jumps to $\log_2|A|$. The information was always there; $\sigma_q$ was the key. - Open the other two tabs to see the which-factor wall and the abelianization cap for the group you chose. --- ## 2. Wall one: the abelianization cap The residue takes $[G:G']$ values. By Lagrange's theorem each coset of $G'$ has the same size, so the residue is *uniform* and its entropy is exactly $\log_2[G:G']$. A variable with that much entropy can share at most that many bits with anything: $$I(\psi\circ c;\ \varphi\circ T)\ \le\ I(c;T)\ \le\ \log_2[G:G'].$$ The first inequality is the [data processing inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing_inequality): coarsening either side never helps. {{visualization:0}} For $S_4$, with five splitting types and 24 elements, the cap is **one bit**, namely the sign of $\sigma_p$. Perfect groups such as $A_5$ have cap **zero**.
Proof of the cap, and when it is attained $I(c;T) = H(c) - H(c\mid T) \le H(c)$. Every fibre of $c$ is a coset $gG'$ of size $|G'|$, so $c$ is uniform on $|G|/|G'|$ values and $H(c) = \log_2[G:G']$. Equality holds iff $H(c\mid T)=0$, that is, iff the residue is a function of the type. Since $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}\in G'$, cosets of $G'$ are unions of conjugacy classes, so the Artin class always attains the cap. The cycle type attains it for $S_3$ and $S_4$, but not for $A_4$ ($\approx 0.918$ of $1.585$ bits) or $D_4$ ($\approx 1.656$ of $2$ bits).
The cap computation is fully algorithmic: {{algorithm:1}} --- ## 3. Wall two: which factor is which? Suppose you knew both splitting types but not which prime carries which. The missing information is one bit, $b = [T(\sigma_p) < T(\sigma_q)]$. Every function of $N$ is symmetric under $p\leftrightarrow q$, because $pq = qp$. In a non-abelian group, even the Artin class of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ is symmetric, because $$\sigma_q\sigma_p = \sigma_p^{-1}(\sigma_p\sigma_q)\,\sigma_p .$$ **The Symmetry Wall.** Suppose readout-preserving bijections act transitively on the values of a hidden label. Then the label is exactly uniform and the readout carries *exactly* zero bits about it.
Proof of the symmetry wall A bijection $\pi$ that preserves the readout $k$ and carries label class $a$ onto class $b$ maps the cell $\{w=a,k=c\}$ onto $\{w=b,k=c\}$. So within every $k$-fibre all labels are equally likely: $\Pr[w=a,k=c]\cdot\#\text{labels} = \Pr[k=c]$. Summing over $c$ shows that the label is uniform. Hence $\Pr[w=a,k=c] = \Pr[w=a]\Pr[k=c]$, the joint law factors, and $I(w;k)=0$.
Consequences, valid in **every** finite group: - the which-factor bit has entropy exactly $1$, and every swap-invariant readout carries exactly $0$ bits about it; - with $m+1$ prime factors, "which factor has the smallest type" carries exactly $\log_2(m+1)$ bits, and every readout symmetric under transpositions carries exactly $0$ of them; - the *ordered* readout $(T\sigma_p, T\sigma_q)$ recovers the full bit, so the wall is not vacuous. The wall can be certified without computing a single logarithm: {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 4. Wall three: the Frobenius one-time pad This is the strongest of the three. Take $\sigma_p$ uniform on *any* candidate set $A\subseteq G$ and $\sigma_q$ uniform on $G$. The shear $$(x,y)\longmapsto(x,\;xy)$$ is a bijection of $A\times G$. So $(\sigma_p,\sigma_p\sigma_q)$ is uniform on $A\times G$, and its two coordinates are independent. This is precisely how a [one-time pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-time_pad) works, with $\sigma_q$ as the key. **The Frobenius One-Time Pad.** In any finite group, abelian or not, every readout of $\sigma_p\sigma_q$ carries exactly zero bits about every readout of $\sigma_p$. After any observation, the posterior equals the prior. {{visualization:1}}
Proof via the shear count For predicates $P,Q$ on $G$, the map $(x,z)\mapsto(x,x^{-1}z)$ is a bijection from $\{x\in A: P(x)\}\times\{z\in G: Q(z)\}$ onto $\{(x,y)\in A\times G: P(x)\wedge Q(xy)\}$. Write $\alpha_a = \#\{x\in A: F(x)=a\}$ and $\beta_b = \#\{z\in G: H(z)=b\}$. Then the joint cell has $\alpha_a\beta_b$ elements and the marginals have $\alpha_a|G|$ and $|A|\beta_b$. So $$\#\{F=a,H=b\}\cdot|A\times G| = \#\{F=a\}\cdot\#\{H=b\},$$ which is the counting form of independence, and therefore $I=0$ exactly. The weaker "no pruning" statement follows at once: for any target $\sigma$ and any candidate $x$, the element $y = x^{-1}\sigma$ satisfies $xy=\sigma$. So every candidate survives.
The exact channel evaluator, with its integer certificate of independence, is the workhorse behind every zero on this page: {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 5. The semiprime ledger: pure synergy Put the three walls together on the full space $G\times G$, with $\rho$ the residue of $N$: | quantity | value | |---|---| | $H(\rho)$ | exactly $\log_2[G:G']$ (uniform) | | $I(\rho;\ \text{type of } p)$, $I(\rho;\ \text{type of } q)$ | exactly $0$ (one-time pad + swap) | | $I(\rho;\ \text{ordered pair}) - I(\rho;\ \text{unordered pair})$ | exactly $0$ (symmetry wall on each fibre) | | $I(\rho;\ \text{anything})$ | $\le \log_2[G:G']$ (cap) | For $S_4$ the residue knows exactly $1$ bit about the unordered pair of types. For $D_4$ it knows $\tfrac{39}{16}-\tfrac34\log_2 3+\tfrac{5}{64}\log_2 5\approx 1.430$ bits. All of it is **synergistic**: none of it is visible to a reader of either factor alone, and none of it says which factor is which. Check these numbers in tab ③ of the laboratory, or run the full demonstration: {{demo:0}} --- ## 6. Where the walls end
The honest seams 1. The cap bounds *residue* content. A readout that does not factor through $G/G'$ is bounded only by the entropy of the type. 2. The wall assumes symmetry. A side input that treats $p$ and $q$ asymmetrically is untouched, but no such input computable from $N$ is known. 3. The model treats Frobenius elements as exactly uniform. For real primes of a given size this is an effective Chebotarev question, with explicit error terms known under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. A surviving method must therefore supply, all at once, a readout of $p$ that (i) escapes the abelianization, (ii) breaks the $p\leftrightarrow q$ symmetry, and (iii) yields more than $O(1)$ bits about which factor is which, all from $N$ alone. By the one-time pad, (i) alone is not enough.
The Galois/Frobenius side channel turns out to be a fifth family of ideas about factoring, distinct from congruences of squares, group orders, smoothness and special curves. In the uniform model, the three walls close it.
